clue.text: Bewildered Euclidean left to go like the clappers?

indicators.note: bewildered means confused, so the remaining letters of the word are jumbled
to go tells us the piece named just before must leave the word

explanation.surface: A baffled Euclidean is told to leave and go off at top speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go like the clappers' is British slang for moving very fast, but here 'the clappers' alone is the definition. 'left to go' removes L from EUCLIDEAN, leaving EUCIDEAN, which 'Bewildered' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectators at a show applaud, so the people clapping are the assembled spectators.

clue.text: Perhaps Oxford bags inch too wide, the ends of which required …

indicators.note: the ends of these four words are taken, one final letter from each

explanation.surface: Wide Oxford bags trousers are an inch too roomy, and something is needed to finish them off.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford bags are baggy trousers, but an Oxford is also a lace-up style of footwear; 'Perhaps' marks it as an example. The clue runs on into the next one.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxford is a classic lace-up example of footwear, hence 'Perhaps'.

clue.text: … and the end of which required to walk up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to pace is to walk

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: and its tip is needed for walking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which' refers back to the previous answer, the footwear, so its end is the reinforced tip. 'up' turns PACE into ECAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A reinforced cap covers the front tip of a boot, the end of the footwear.

clue.text: Official residence making a packet? (You have been warned!)

definitions.meaning: the residence of an ambassador abroad
A British cigarette brand, sold in packets carrying health warnings

explanation.surface: A grand official residence turns out to be making a fortune, and you were warned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making a packet' suggests earning lots of money; the packet is literally a cigarette packet, and 'You have been warned!' nods to the government health warning printed on it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambassador's official home and offices abroad go by this name, as did a cigarette brand.

clue.text: Navigator capsized vessels indulging in kinky vice

indicators.note: the vice letters take in the turned vessels, so they surround them
kinky means twisted, so the letters of vice are rearranged
capsized means turned upside down, so in a down clue the word is reversed

parts.note: cups are drinking vessels

explanation.surface: A sailor's boats overturn while he indulges in perverted habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessels' suggests ships for a navigator, but these are drinking vessels. Amerigo Vespucci was the Italian explorer who gave America its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Amerigo Vespucci was a famous Italian explorer and navigator of the New World.

clue.text: Creatures which may have gone slippery in fishermen's traps?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit inside the traps word

parts.note: creels are wicker baskets used as fish or lobster traps

indicators.note: slippery suggests the letters slide around into a new order

explanation.surface: Some animals may have slithered away from the anglers' baskets.
explanation.walkthrough: Eels are notoriously slippery, so 'slippery' doubles as a fitting surface word while signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Large marine eels of this kind are sea creatures.

clue.text: Briefly visit shops perhaps from home, returning to get purse

indicators.note: returning means the word is turned back, read upwards in this down clue

parts.note: in means at home
to purse the lips is to pout

explanation.surface: Someone pops out from home to the shops and comes back with a new handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purse' looks like a noun, a handbag, but it is the verb: to purse one's lips is to POUT. 'returning' turns IN into NI.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a quick trip out, for instance to the shops, is a common British idiom.

clue.text: Thematically I'm buttonless, as there wasn't ____

definitions.text: Thematically I'm buttonless, as there wasn't ____

parts.words: Thematically I'm buttonless, as there wasn't ____
parts.note: the theme item speaks: it is not the small button variety, as space was short; the blank, read as two words, means not much space

explanation.surface: A theme item explains it never got its button because it ran out of space.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank reads as two words, MUSH ROOM, sounding like 'much room'; a button is a young closed-cap stage of this fungus. This answer is the theme for the clues numbered 8.
explanation.definitionFit: The button is the small young stage of this fungus, so a grown one has lost its button form.

clue.text: 8 eaten by carnivore? No kidding!

indicators.note: eaten by says the answer is swallowed within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fungus is devoured by a meat-eater, and that is no joke.
explanation.walkthrough: '8' refers to the theme answer, so the definition is a type of edible fungus. The answer runs across carnivorE NO KIdding.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoki are thin white Japanese edible fungi, a kind of the theme answer at 8.

clue.text: Sensible letters read out

indicators.note: read out means the letters are spoken, so their sound is what counts

parts.note: the letters are a pair of Ys

explanation.surface: Someone sensibly reads out a sequence of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letter Ys, said aloud, sound like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensible and wise are close synonyms describing sound judgement.

clue.text: 8 food and its source, a quarter in blue

indicators.note: in tells us the food, its source and the quarter go inside the blue piece

parts.note: blue is the colour of the Conservatives, abbreviated Con
ham is a food
ham comes from a pig
N, for north, is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: A fungus is food that comes from somewhere, a quarter of it in blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative party; the quarter is a compass point. The food and its source go in after the first letter of the party abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Champignon is the French word for a cultivated edible fungus, one of the theme answer at 8.

clue.text: See 21
Source of oil — raise river bed first by lots

indicators.note: first by puts the bed at the front, followed by the lots

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
tons means lots

indicators.note: raise, in a down clue, lifts the word so it reads upwards

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and in Wales

explanation.surface: To get oil, raise the riverbed first by plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'river bed' looks like one thing but splits into the river and the bed; 'raise' turns the river upward in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil is pressed from the seeds of the cotton plant, used in cooking.

clue.text: Cover chastity, not head, after brief moment

indicators.note: after puts the shortened chastity word behind the brief moment

parts.note: sec is a short form of second, a brief moment

indicators.note: not head means the first letter is removed

parts.note: purity means chastity

explanation.surface: Insurance cover for virtue, of the beheaded kind, arrives a moment later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not head' removes P from PURITY to leave URITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurance-style cover, or protection, is another word for safeguarding against harm.

clue.text: Police set about invading Watford area (roundabout)

indicators.note: invading means the rearranged letters get inside the area word

parts.note: Watford Gap is a gap in the hills in Northamptonshire, known for its motorway services

indicators.note: about signals the letters of set are moved around

parts.note: a roundabout is circular, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Police surround a group invading the Watford district near a traffic roundabout.
explanation.walkthrough: Watford Gap is an English motorway service area, so 'Watford area' is the gap rather than a postcode or district; the bracketed roundabout supplies the final circle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gestapo was the secret state police of Nazi Germany.

clue.text: Touching and panting when writhing, embracing love

indicators.note: embracing means the rearranged letters hold the next piece inside
writhing means twisting about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A moving scene of heavy breathing and squirming in a lovers' embrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writhing' rearranges PANTING to PIGNANT, which takes in O after the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Something touching stirs the emotions, as a poignant moment does.

clue.text: Dalai Lama, for instance, finds Greek character canned?

annotationWithheld.why: Dalai Lama, for instance, finds Greek character canned? (7): BETA inside TIN, but 'canned' gives both TIN and the containment, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Dalai Lama, for instance, finds Greek character canned?

clue.text: First creature on an opening leaf looked up?

definitions.text: First creature on an opening leaf looked up?

parts.words: First creature on an opening leaf looked up?
parts.note: the opening page of a dictionary, where words are looked up, begins with this animal's name

explanation.surface: The first animal one sees on the first page of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaf' is a page, and 'looked up' means consulted in a dictionary; this African burrowing mammal heads most English dictionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: This African anteater is famously the first animal listed alphabetically in a dictionary.

clue.text: 8 providing benefit without success

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the benefit word goes around

parts.note: for one's sake means for one's benefit
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A fungus brings benefit, though without success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside, its old sense. The answer is a Japanese fungus, more often spelt shiitake.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiitake are Japanese edible fungi, a kind of the theme answer at 8.

clue.text: To stagger is not to crash into tree

indicators.note: into means the rearranged letters are put inside the tree

parts.note: the ash is a tree

indicators.note: crash suggests the letters smash into a new order

explanation.surface: A driver staggers, insisting he did not crash into a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' belongs to the surface sentence; the definition is the verb 'stagger', meaning to amaze.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagger someone is to amaze or stun them, a close synonym.

clue.text: 8 giving sea bird severe pain circling old South American rock, finally swallowed

parts.note: the shag is a sea bird, a kind of cormorant

indicators.note: circling means the pain word goes around the next piece

parts.note: gyp is British slang for severe pain, as in 'my back is giving me gyp'

indicators.note: swallowed means the letter goes inside the South American word

parts.note: the Incas were an ancient South American people

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of rock

explanation.surface: A fungus gives a seabird terrible pain, wrapping around an ancient Peruvian who has swallowed a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Gyp is British slang for pain ('my knee is giving me gyp'); the rock's last letter goes inside the Inca, and the pain wraps the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: The shaggy ink cap is a common edible fungus, one of the theme answer at 8.

clue.text: Eatery with inventive Hungarian stew half eaten

indicators.note: eaten means the half stew goes inside the inventor's name

parts.note: Laszlo Biro was the Hungarian inventor of the ballpoint pen

indicators.note: half takes the first two of the four letters of stew

explanation.surface: A restaurant serves a creative Hungarian goulash, partly eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: Hungarian suggests goulash, but it is Laszlo Biro, inventor of the ballpoint pen, whose name became the British word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal restaurant or eatery.

clue.text: 8 missed the opportunity?

definitions.meaning: a kind of the theme answer: an edible fungus with a lilac stem
to fluff a chance, as in the phrase 'messed it up'

explanation.surface: A fungus missed its big chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer is BLEW IT, slang for wasting a chance.
explanation.definitionFit: Blewits are edible fungi, and split in two the word means wasted a chance.

clue.text: Little house on estate I'm developing

indicators.note: developing suggests the letters are being built into something new

explanation.surface: A small home on a housing estate is something I'm building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developing' rearranges ON ESTATE I'M. The estate is a housing estate, fitting the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A maisonette is a small flat or house, literally a little house in French.

clue.text: Rascal beheaded one in cathedral …

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: a knave is a rascal

explanation.surface: A rogue is executed inside a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beheaded' removes K from KNAVE. The clue runs on into the next one.
explanation.definitionFit: The nave is the central body of a cathedral, one of its main parts.

clue.text: Bomb (some inhuman UK export)

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A bomb is some inhuman item that Britain sells abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuke is informal for a nuclear weapon, a type of bomb.

clue.text: … when I entered, Lincoln?

definitions.meaning: the previous answer with I put inside gives a word for inexperienced
Lincoln is a famous shade of this colour, worn by Robin Hood's men

explanation.surface: Continuing: when I went into Lincoln Cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: Linked to the previous clue: put I into that answer to get NAIVE, which means inexperienced, the first sense. Lincoln green is the cloth colour of Robin Hood's band.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexperienced people are called this colour, and Lincoln gives its name to a shade of it.

clue.text: Exclamation of contempt for burglars sounded

indicators.note: sounded means the word is said aloud and heard

parts.note: to nick is to steal, so burglars are nickers

explanation.surface: A scornful exclamation about some housebreakers, voiced aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knickers!' is a dated British exclamation of contempt or annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: Knickers is British slang used as an exclamation of disbelief or contempt.
